title: DFS on Barcelona: Real Street Routing ⚡
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) dive through Barcelona’s Eixample grid like a stack-driven explorer—choosing one street branch, then backtracking when it hits dead ends. This visualization turns graph traversal into street-level intuition you can reuse on LeetCode graph theory problems.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps — what happens when DFS explores city intersections ⚡

In this visualization, every intersection is a node and every street segment is an edge (a graph). DFS takes one path “deep” using a stack/recursion feel, marks visited nodes, and only backtracks when the current route can’t continue.

Why it matters:
- Great for understanding graph traversal order
- Highlights backtracking mechanics (the “try → go deep → return” loop)
- Turns “dfs algorithm explained” into something you can *see*

Takeaway: DFS doesn’t look for the shortest route—its goal is to fully explore depth-first, so ordering/neighbor choices can change the traversal.

Debate question: If two neighbor choices exist, should your DFS pick the “leftmost street” first—or the “closest to destination” street first?
